title: Names of God in the Granth
word: Names of God in the Granth
hook: Waheguru, Ram, Hari, Gobind, Allah, Khuda, Prabh, Akal: the Granth uses many

segments.voice: Yesterday we closed the streams: orders, schools, communities, places and music. Your line was many streams. Which stream did you name as the one you'd visit? Day one thousand three hundred sixty-two.

A new part of the year starts today: Sikh thought. Not the history, not the places, but the big ideas underneath them. And the first idea is a question a child might ask in the back of a gurdwara: what is God's name? Sit through a morning of reading from the Guru Granth Sahib with that question in your pocket, and the answer keeps changing. One hymn says Hari. The next says Ram. Then Gobind, then Prabh, the Lord. In some hymns the word is Allah, or Khuda. A single book, read out from one cloth-covered stand, calls on the One by name after name. Today's lesson is that crowd of names.
screen: `A NEW PART: SIKH THOUGHT.` → `WHAT IS GOD'S NAME?` → `HARI, RAM, GOBIND, ALLAH, KHUDA.`

segments.voice: Start with the pages. The Granth gathers hymns from the Gurus and from other saints, and they reach for the language their listeners already used. So the One is Hari and Ram and Gobind, names from the devotional songs listeners already knew, and also Allah and Khuda, words their Muslim neighbors prayed with. The opening line of the Granth adds names of its own: the Timeless Form, Akal Murat, and the creator who is without fear and without hate. Why so many? Guru Arjan has a line about exactly this, in a hymn in Raag Maru. In paraphrase: my tongue speaks the names that describe what You have done, but True Name is Your name from before everything. The names we use, the Guru says, are names of deeds: the one who sustains, the one who protects, the one who made the world. Each catches one thing the One does. None catches the One. Then there's what a name means here. When Sikhs read Ram in the Granth, they read it as the One who is present in everything, not as one figure from one story. The names point past themselves. And there's what this does to a listener. Sikh readers draw a plain lesson from a book that says Allah and Hari side by side: nobody owns the word for God, and no name has to be defended against another. A name is a door, not a fence. One name sits at the center of Sikh daily prayer, and tomorrow is about that one. But the Granth keeps the crowd. Many names.
screen: `THE GRANTH SPEAKS MANY NAMES.` · `NAMES OF DEEDS, NOT THE WHOLE ONE.` · `TRUE NAME IS FROM BEFORE.` · `A NAME IS A DOOR, NOT A FENCE.` · then, large: `MANY NAMES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: write the names you know. Settle, and breathe. On paper, or in your head, list every name for God you've ever heard, from any language, any home, any song. Don't sort them or judge them. Just let them line up. Then look at the list and notice each one as a door someone walked through. If you pray, you can choose one name and repeat it gently for the rest of the sit. If you don't, just breathe with the list in front of you. The bell holds the time.
Names of God in the Granth. Hari, Ram, Gobind, Prabh, Allah, Khuda, Akal and more: names of what the One does, pointing past themselves to the One. Today's word.
screen: `NAMES OF GOD IN THE GRANTH — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: many names. Today, when you hear someone speak of God in words that aren't yours, let the word be a door, not a fence. Day one thousand three hundred sixty-two.

howItsDone: In gurdwaras the Guru Granth Sahib is read aloud, and listeners hear the One called by many names, among them Hari, Ram, Gobind, Prabh, Allah and Khuda, all read as names of the same One.
